questions.q: According to this lesson, what makes a class a good fit for a piece of quant code?
options: Any time a computation involves more than one function
The presence of state that persists and changes over time, combined with behavior tied to that state
Whenever NumPy arrays are involved
Whenever the code needs to run fast
questions.explain: The lesson's test is whether there's genuine persisting state with behavior attached to it (like a PositionBook updating as fills arrive) -- not just whether something *could* be written as a class.

questions.q: Why must `positions: dict = field(default_factory=dict)` be used instead of `positions: dict = {}` in a dataclass?
options: Because dataclasses don't support dict fields at all
Because a bare mutable default like `{}` would be shared across every instance of the class; `default_factory` creates a fresh dict per instance
Because `default_factory` makes the field immutable
Because dict fields require a custom __eq__ method
questions.explain: Mutable default arguments in Python are evaluated once and shared across all instances, which would cause every PositionBook to share the same dict; default_factory avoids this by creating a new dict for each instance.

questions.q: In the real measured comparison between a dataclass instance and a `__slots__` instance, why did a naive `sys.getsizeof()` comparison understate the dataclass's true memory footprint?
options: sys.getsizeof() always returns 0 for dataclasses
sys.getsizeof() on a regular object doesn't include the size of its separate __dict__ object, which has to be added separately for a fair comparison
__slots__ objects cannot be measured with sys.getsizeof()
The dataclass had fewer fields than the __slots__ class
questions.explain: A regular object's __dict__ is a separate object in memory; sys.getsizeof(obj) alone doesn't count it. Once added in (sys.getsizeof(obj) + sys.getsizeof(obj.__dict__)), the real total for the dataclass instance was 152 bytes vs. 56 bytes for the __slots__ version.

questions.q: What behavioral side effect does `__slots__` have, beyond saving memory?
options: It makes all attributes read-only
It blocks assigning any attribute not explicitly declared in __slots__, raising an AttributeError instead of silently creating a new one
It automatically converts all attributes to properties
It disables the __init__ method
questions.explain: Because __slots__ instances have no per-instance __dict__, attempting to set an attribute not listed in __slots__ raises AttributeError -- which can catch typos but also means code relying on ad hoc attributes won't work.

questions.q: According to the lesson, what is the recommended default relationship between two classes that share some behavior, when there isn't a genuine 'is-a' relationship?
options: Always use multiple inheritance
Composition -- one object holds and delegates to another, rather than inheriting from it
Copy-paste the shared code into both classes
Convert both classes into global functions
questions.explain: The lesson recommends composition as the safer default, reserving inheritance for genuine is-a relationships with behavior that naturally varies by subtype, like a Strategy base class.
